newsitem.title: CHINA: Shenzhen property seen providing interim contrast.
newsitem.headline: Shenzhen property seen providing interim contrast.

text.p: A pick-up in residential property demand in the south China boom town of Shenzhen will contrast sharply with the stagnating office market when real estate firms release their 1997 interim results, analysts said on Wednesday.

Residential property developers in Shenzhen would see a further recovery in interim earnings, aided by official policy and strengthening individual demand, analysts told the Hong Kong-based newsletter China Securities Bulletin.
However, companies mainly involved in office construction were likely to continue to report weak first-half results due to a glut in the sector, they said.
Shenzhen, bordering on the former British colony of Hong Kong, has about a dozen major property firms which are also listed on the local bourse.
"Many office buildings have been vacant for years even though many of them were completed a few years ago," said an analyst at a foreign investment bank in Shenzhen.

About 63.4 percent of Shenzhen's office buildings were empty by the end of 1996, and only 140,000 square metres (1.5 million sq ft) of office space was sold last year, far below residential property sales, the Shenzhen Special Zone Daily has reported.

Demand for office space was dampened by the central government's moves to phase out preferential treatment for foreign-funded enterprises in Shenzhen and spiralling land prices, the foreign bank analyst said.
More foreign-funded firms and enterprises had moved out of Shenzhen to take advantage of lower operating costs.

"Shenzhen's office market remained stagnant in the first half of this year," said a spokesman for developer Shenzhen Special Economic Zone Real Estate & Properties (Group) Co Ltd. "There is still a large amount of empty office space," he said.
The company posted a net loss of 26 million yuan under international accounting standards for 1996 and blamed the loss on poor sales in the boom-and-bust Shenzhen real estate market.

A property investment boom in China, especially in Shenzhen and the island province of Hainan, blossomed in the early 1990s before Beijing launched a three-year credit clampdown in 1993 aimed largely at the country's speculative property sector.
The credit squeeze left property developers with fewer buyers and tenants amid falling sales and prices.

China's two cuts in lending rates last year may have eased the interest payment burdens of property firms, but the impact was limited by a high asset-to-debt ratio of an average 65 percent at the end of 1996, official statistics have shown.
But the residential market looked brighter, analysts said.
The number of individual home buyers in Shenzhen had swelled after a 1996 share market bull run created a rich property-owning class, a Shenzhen J&A Securities analyst said.
A proliferation of mortgage loan services provided by state commercial banks made it easier for Shenzhen people to buy commercial property, analysts said.
China's state banks would provide about 10 billion yuan (US$1.2 billion) in mortgage loans this year, with terms of up to 20 years and 70 percent of cost, official media has said.
Analysts said listed firms with substantial land reserves in Shenzhen had strong growth potential because the city's proximity to Hong Kong would make it a magnet for home buyers.

"But there won't be a remarkable improvement (in the interim earnings of listed residential property developers)," the J&A analyst said. "China's real estate sector is just picking up from its lowest point."
